items.title: Declarations of Pecuniary Interest under the “Municipal Conflict of Interest Act”
Scott Stager Piatkowski, Waterloo
notes: S. Stager Piatkowski appeared before the Committee to speak to the election sign by-law, expressing support for the existing regulations. He provided further comments on his position, including opposition to election signs on regional roads.

items.title: Peter Woolstencroft, Waterloo
notes:
P. Woolstencroft appeared before the Committee to speak to the staff report on election signs and provided comments in support of maintaining the current approach.

The Committee discussed trends in civic engagement and voter participation. Members considered the role of the education system in fostering an understanding of citizenship, including rights and responsibilities, and how this may influence voter turnout.

The Committee also examined the potential impact of lowering the voting age as a means to engage younger voters. Perspectives were shared on the importance of education in preparing individuals for participation in the electoral process. The concept of mandatory voting, as practiced in some countries, was also discussed in relation to its potential effects on voter engagement.

Further discussion took place regarding opportunities to enhance voter education. It was suggested that additional learning initiatives be explored, particularly during election years, and that the Clerk’s office consider offering more educational sessions.

items.title: Brenden Sherratt, Kitchener
notes:
B. Sherratt appeared before the Committee to speak to the election sign by-law. He emphasized that staff should focus on other priorities beyond measuring the distance between signs, such as road safety in high-traffic areas and the risks campaign volunteers face when stopping on the road to place signs. He also mentioned traffic safety concerns, the shift in modern campaigning away from physical election signs, and the benefits of encouraging social media advertising, town halls, and other forms of outreach. He noted that the existing by-law is effective in reducing waste, eliminating sign-related conflicts, and improving road safety. He also pointed out that 90 percent of incumbents are re-elected.

Committee members engaged in a discussion, sharing their perspectives and drawing on their personal experiences with door-knocking.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Resilient and Future Ready Organization
PDL-CAS-25-005, Election Sign By-law
notes:
William Short, Director Council and Administrative Services/Regional Clerk introduced the report, noting that it was being presented for information. He highlighted that the report did not address voter turnout or whether election signs influence turnout and mentioned that there is no available data from Elections Ontario on this matter. He further spoke to the by-laws and the amendments made over the years and noted discussions with by-law staff. It was clarified that staff would continue to receive the same number of calls regardless of the by-law. The information from both reports has been consolidated and is now in the hands of Council.

Members of the Committee deliberated on the report. There were considerations raised regarding potential barriers related to election signs and their impact on different communities. It was noted that the report should encompass a broader perspective, including not only financial factors but also other considerations that may affect certain groups.

The status quo was discussed in terms of its potential effects on incumbents.

A motion was proposed to prepare a by-law to repeal the prohibition of election signs. The motion was defeated.

The Committee raised concerns that the wording in Section D of the report was inappropriate and did not reflect a proper understanding of the issue. It was also noted that the language presented an inaccurate depiction of the matter and, in some instances, perpetuated negative stereotypes about certain demographics. The Committee requested that the wording be revisited in the 2025 report to ensure it is accurate, inclusive, and aligned with current understanding.

The report was received for information.
